questions.q: What does `git push origin main` do?
options: Uploads any local commits on main that the remote doesn't have yet
Downloads commits from the remote
Permanently deletes the remote repository
Creates a new branch on the remote called origin
questions.explain: Push sends your local commits to the named remote and branch.

questions.q: What does `git push -u origin main` set up that a plain `git push` doesn't, the first time you push a new branch?
options: It deletes the local branch after pushing
It links the local branch to that remote branch (the "upstream"), so future git push/pull calls know where to go without repeating the remote and branch name
It makes the branch private
It force-overwrites the remote's history
questions.explain: The --set-upstream flag records the tracking relationship, simplifying every push and pull afterward.

questions.q: What does `git fetch` change about your working files or current branch?
options: It immediately merges every remote change into your current branch
It deletes any uncommitted changes
It force-pushes your local commits to the remote
Nothing — it only updates your local record of where the remote's branches are, without touching your working files
questions.explain: Fetch is deliberately non-destructive — it's purely informational until you decide to merge or rebase.

questions.q: What is the key difference between `git pull` and `git fetch`?
options: They are identical; pull is just an older name for fetch
pull only works on private repositories
pull does what fetch does, then immediately merges (or rebases) the changes into your current branch; fetch stops after downloading
fetch uploads your commits, while pull downloads them
questions.explain: Pull automatically integrates the fetched changes, which is convenient but can surprise you with an unexpected merge conflict.

questions.q: Why might you run `git fetch` before `git pull`, as a practical habit?
options: fetch is required before pull will even run
To see what's changed on the remote with zero risk before deciding to merge it in, avoiding an unexpected conflict
fetch is faster and makes pull unnecessary
Because pull doesn't work without an internet connection but fetch does
questions.explain: Fetching first lets you preview incoming changes before pull's automatic merge step integrates them.
